newsitem.title: JAPAN: Giant Nomura sprang from money changer roots.
newsitem.headline: Giant Nomura sprang from money changer roots.

text.p: Nomura Securities Co Ltd has been at the heart of Japan's financial system from the days of its 19th century founding by a money changer to its present giant corporate status.

On Tuesday, the company's once proud reputation took a new battering, when Japan's securities watchdog filed complaints with prosecutors alleging the brokerage and three former executives illegally compensated a corporate client for losses.

The action, the first step in bringing legal action against a company or an individual, followed the resignation last month of the company's president and 15 board members in a scandal involving payoffs to a racketeer.

The present firm, which employs nearly 11,000 staff in dozens of offices around the world and dominates both share and bond trading in Japan, sprang from an Osaka money changing shop set up in 1872 by Tokushichi Nomura, the illegitimate son of a samurai, or Japanese warrior.
His son, Tokushichi Nomura II, enlarged the business and incorporated it in 1925 as Osaka Nomura Bank.
The son, who died in 1945, was an acknowledged financial wizard whose gains in share dealings earned him the name, "The Great General of the Stock Market".
Nomura Securities grew out of the breakup of the bank.
It started by trading bonds, expanding into securities in 1938, and in 1941 became the first Japanese firm to start investment trust operations.

Most of the Nomura fortune was lost in the ruins of World War Two. But the firm, no longer family owned, quickly recovered and achieved global prominence by underwriting companies such as Sony Corp that were at the heart of Japan's postwar economic miracle.
In 1969, as a key component of a relentless overseas expansion, the firm set up Nomura Securities International in the United States. In 1972, it set up Nomura Europe.
It exerts a powerful influence on every business in the yen bond market and is also Japan's top foreign bond seller.

In a previous scandal in 1991, Nomura and other leading Japanese brokerages were found to be paying improper compensation to favoured clients. Top executives at Nomura resigned in 1991 over the improper compensation and revelations that affiliates had done deals with gangsters.
